**BARCELONA, Spain (CNN)** — Google launched the latest salvo in the fiercely contested smartphone market on Tuesday, unveiling its newest Android-powered handset designed to go head-to-head with Apple’s iPhone. 

Introduced at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, the Vodafone-backed HTC Magic smartphone is scheduled to make its European debut in the United Kingdom, Spain, France, and Germany in the coming months, followed by a non-exclusive launch in Italy. 

Android-powered devices are widely regarded as the primary rivals to Apple's iPhone in the battle to define the next generation of mobile technology. For many industry observers, Google’s latest foray into the market signals the tech giant's broader ambition to dominate the mobile sector. However, this expansion has raised concerns among critics, who question whether device manufacturers, network operators, and end-users will retain sufficient control over the data Google extracts through its software.

Among the prominent skeptics is the LiMo Foundation—developer of the competing Linux-based LiMo platform—as highlighted in the daily newsletter published by event organizer Groupe Speciale Mobile Association (GSMA). 

"A lot of operators still harbor some questions over whether they will have the control over services and how much of the data that is going out and coming from a Google device goes to Google and how much to you [the operator]," Andrew Shikiar of the LiMo Foundation told *Mobile Business Briefing*.

Much like the iPhone, Android devices allow users to download third-party software, effectively turning the handsets into powerful, pocket-sized computers. The HTC Magic builds on the momentum of the G1, the very first Android-capable device, which launched last year in partnership with T-Mobile as Google's initial entry into the European market via the UK.

Technically, the HTC Magic features a 3.2-inch QVGA touchscreen display, tactile navigation buttons, and a trackball. It comes pre-loaded with a suite of native Google applications, including Gmail, Google Maps, Google Search, and YouTube.

Andy Rubin, Senior Director of Mobile Platforms at Google, characterized the release of the HTC Magic as a pivotal milestone for the Android ecosystem. 

"With it, Vodafone is opening up the mobile web for consumers across Europe and giving more third-party developers a platform on which they can build the next wave of killer applications," Rubin stated.

CNN’s Adrian Finighan, reporting from the congress, noted that as a dedicated iPhone user, he spent much of the event seeking a genuine contender to Apple's flagship device. 

"The Magic is, well, magic! I think I've found it," Finighan observed. "It really is the first device that I could consider swapping my beloved Apple device for."

**Google Takes the Fight to Apple with European Launch of the HTC Magic**

Google has officially fired its next major salvo in the high-stakes battle for mobile supremacy. Partnering with global telecom giant Vodafone, the search titan has announced the European rollout of the HTC Magic, its second-generation Android-powered device. The strategic release marks a direct challenge to Apple’s iPhone, positioning Google as the primary alternative in the rapidly expanding next-generation smartphone market.

Sleeker and more refined than its predecessor—the T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream)—the HTC Magic sheds the bulky physical keyboard in favor of a sleek, touch-only interface that directly mirrors the aesthetic appeal of the iPhone. Powered by Google’s open-source Android operating system, the device provides users with seamless, out-of-the-box integration with Google’s core suite of services, including Google Search, Maps, Gmail, and YouTube. By securing an exclusive distribution deal with Vodafone across key European markets, including the UK, Spain, Germany, and Italy, Google is ensuring that its operating system gains an immediate, footprint-expanding foothold across the continent.

The launch firmly establishes Google as Apple’s chief competitor in the mobile space, setting up a fundamental clash of business philosophies. While Apple maintains strict, end-to-end control over both its hardware and software through a "walled garden" approach, Google is employing a Trojan-horse strategy: offering Android free to hardware manufacturers to build a massive, interconnected ecosystem. By enabling hardware partners like HTC to deliver competitive devices, Google aims to commoditize smartphone software and rapidly scale its global market share.

However, Google’s aggressive expansion into mobile infrastructure has reignited fierce industry debate and heightened anxieties regarding the company’s expanding reach. Unlike Apple, which generates the vast majority of its mobile revenue through hardware margins, Google’s core business relies on ad monetization driven by consumer information. Industry analysts and privacy advocates have raised alarm over the sheer volume of personal data Google stands to collect through Android devices, which seamlessly track location data, search queries, app usage, and web browsing habits. 

Furthermore, carrier partners themselves harbor lingering reservations. As Google embeds its search engine and web services deeper into the mobile layer, telecommunication networks fear being reduced to mere "dumb pipes"—providing the expensive cellular infrastructure while Google captures the most lucrative data streams and digital ad revenue.

Despite these growing pains and regulatory headwinds, the arrival of the HTC Magic signals a defining moment in the evolution of personal computing. As the device hits European storefronts, the mobile landscape officially transitions into a two-horse race. Whether Google’s open-source model and data-driven ecosystem can ultimately outpace Apple’s premium, closed platform remains the defining question of the smartphone era.

**BARCELONA, Spain (CNN)** — The battle for smartphone supremacy reached a fever pitch Tuesday at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, as Taiwanese manufacturer HTC unveiled its new "Magic" handset—a sleek, all-touchscreen device powered by Google’s Android operating system that takes aim squarely at Apple’s iPhone.

The HTC Magic marks the second commercial device to run on Google’s open-source mobile software, following the late-2008 launch of the T-Mobile G1 (also known as the HTC Dream). 

However, while the G1 was criticized by some for its bulky design and slide-out physical keyboard, the HTC Magic drops the hardware keys entirely in favor of a slim, glossy profile. The shift in design makes no secret of the company’s ambitions: Google and HTC are coming directly for the iPhone's crown.

### A sleeker challenger

Featuring a 3.2-inch capacitive touchscreen, a 3.2-megapixel camera, GPS, and a signature trackball for navigation, the Magic is noticeably thinner and lighter than its predecessor. It boasts full web-browsing capabilities and seamless integration with Google's suite of services, including Gmail, Google Maps, and YouTube.

"The HTC Magic is a major step forward for Android," said Peter Chou, CEO of HTC Corporation, during the press conference in Barcelona. "It delivers a powerful, intuitive mobile internet experience in a form factor that consumers will love."

Industry observers noted that by shedding the keyboard, Google's Android platform has finally achieved the visual and tactile appeal needed to compete in the premium consumer market.

"The first Android phone proved the software worked, but the HTC Magic proves Android can be stylish," said Carolina Milanesi, research director at tech research firm Gartner. "This is the first Android device that poses a direct aesthetic and functional threat to the iPhone."

### The open platform vs. the walled garden

The unveiling underscores a growing clash of philosophies in the tech industry. While Apple maintains strict, end-to-end control over both the iPhone's hardware and software, Google is offering Android as an open-source system available to any hardware manufacturer or carrier.

By expanding the Android ecosystem, Google hopes to replicate its desktop search dominance on mobile devices—ensuring its profitable ad network remains central as consumers shift from PCs to smartphones.

To fuel this expansion, the HTC Magic will feature an upgraded version of the Android Market, Google's answer to Apple's wildly popular App Store, allowing users to download third-party applications over the air.

For carriers eager to break Apple’s exclusive distribution deals—such as AT&T's hold on the iPhone in the United States—Android offers a powerful alternative. European telecom giant Vodafone announced Tuesday that it will exclusively offer the HTC Magic in key markets including the UK, Spain, Germany, France, and Italy starting this spring.

### A crowded battlefield

When Apple launched the iPhone in 2007, it fundamentally disrupted the mobile industry, leaving legacy giants like BlackBerry maker Research In Motion, Nokia, and Microsoft scrambling to react. 

With the launch of the HTC Magic, Google is signaling that it intends to lead the counteroffensive.

While Apple still holds a massive head start in app availability and brand loyalty, analysts say the entrance of well-designed Android hardware like the Magic means the era of absolute iPhone dominance in the touchscreen market may be coming to an end.

"The smartphone war is no longer just about hardware; it's about the software ecosystem," said Milanesi. "Google is building a coalition of manufacturers and carriers. Apple redefined the smartphone in 2007, but 2009 is shaping up to be the year Google fights back."

**HTC Unveils ‘Magic’ Android Smartphone as Vodafone Secures European Launch**

**BARCELONA, Spain — Feb. 17, 2009** — High Tech Computer Corp. (HTC) today officially announced the HTC Magic, the world’s second mobile handset powered by the Google Android operating system. Unveiled at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, the touch-centric device marks a significant evolution from its predecessor, the T-Mobile G1, ditching the physical QWERTY keyboard in favor of a sleeker, slate-style form factor aimed at the consumer mass market.

European telecommunications giant Vodafone has secured exclusive carrier rights for the launch across several key markets, positioning the device as a direct challenger to Apple’s iPhone 3G and Research In Motion’s BlackBerry lineup.

### **Vodafone Secures European Exclusivity**

Under the terms of the agreement, Vodafone will begin rolling out the HTC Magic across Europe in the spring of 2009. The handset will initially be available in the United Kingdom, Spain, Germany, France, and Italy, with availability expanding to additional markets over the coming months. 

Vodafone executives emphasized that the device will be heavily subsidized, offered for free on select monthly contract plans. 

"Introducing the HTC Magic to the European market strengthens our commitment to offering our customers the most innovative mobile internet experience," said Patrick Chomet, Global Director of Terminals at Vodafone. "Android offers a flexible platform for mobile internet services, and we are confident that this handset will appeal to a broad demographic seeking rich multimedia and browsing capabilities."

### **Hardware and Technical Specifications**

Unlike the original HTC Dream (G1), which featured a slide-out keyboard, the HTC Magic relies entirely on a capacitive touchscreen interface, resulting in a noticeably thinner profile measuring just 13.65 mm thick and weighing 118 grams. 

The device retains the signature clickable trackball at the bottom of the front panel for precision navigation. Key hardware specifications confirmed by HTC include:

*   **Display:** 3.2-inch TFT-LCD capacitive touchscreen with HVGA resolution (320 x 480 pixels).
*   **Processor:** Qualcomm MSM7201A running at 528 MHz.
*   **Memory:** 512 MB ROM, 192 MB RAM (with 288 MB RAM featured on select regional variants), expandable via microSD (up to 16 GB).
*   **Camera:** 3.2-megapixel camera with auto-focus (lacking an LED flash).
*   **Connectivity:** 7.2 Mbps HSDPA (3G), Wi-Fi (802.11 b/g), GPS/a-GPS, and Bluetooth 2.0 with A2DP support.
*   **Battery:** 1340 mAh lithium-ion battery.

The handset runs a updated build of the Android platform, featuring an improved virtual keyboard, auto-rotation capabilities via a built-in accelerometer, and seamless integration with Google services such as Maps, Gmail, YouTube, and the Android Market.

### **LiMo Foundation Downplays Threat, Defends Open Standards**

The high-profile debut of HTC’s second Android device has sent ripples through the mobile software industry, prompting a reaction from the LiMo Foundation—the consortium backed by major carriers including NTT DoCoMo, Orange, and Vodafone itself, aimed at creating a open, Linux-based mobile operating system.

While Vodafone’s endorsement of Android represents a potential friction point for LiMo’s unified platform goals, representatives from the LiMo Foundation publicly downplayed concerns regarding Android's market momentum. 

In statements responding to the announcement, LiMo leadership highlighted that while Google's platform utilizes a Linux kernel, it remains a largely single-vendor-driven framework tied to Google's proprietary cloud services. LiMo executives reaffirmed their commitment to a truly neutral, industry-wide open standard governed by operators and manufacturers alike, maintaining that carrier-led initiatives will ultimately provide greater customization and security for global operators than proprietary-leaning open-source models.

Despite LiMo's defensive stance, industry analysts note that the arrival of the HTC Magic signals accelerating momentum for Android, proving that Google's mobile platform is rapidly transitioning from an experimental developer tool into a mainstream commercial power.
